case_info.scenario: A healthy 25-year-old female presented with an 8-month history of a painful right mandibular lesion (Figure 1A). The patient reported progressive persistent pain and enlargement of the lesion since it was first noticed. She denied any facial trauma history and had no sensory deficits in the inferior alveolar nerve distribution or signs of infection such as purulent discharge, foul taste, warmth, or erythema of the overlying skin. She had multiple prior emergency department encounters for this lesion, and maxillofacial computed tomography revealed a multiloculated radiolucent lesion situated below the inferior alveolar nerve at the right mandibular angle (Figure 1B). On clinical examination, there was firm, tender external swelling of the right gonial angle along the inferior border. Intraoral findings were unremarkable, with no drainage or evident expansion into the retromolar trigone. An incisional biopsy was performed via a transoral approach. The intralesional content appeared to be dark brown and spongy. A portion of the tissue was sent for frozen section analysis, which revealed the presence of multinucleated giant cells and spindle cells but was nondiagnostic. A fluorescence in situ hybridization study was subsequently performed, confirming a positiveUSP6gene rearrangement.

case_info.explanation: An aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC) is a benign lesion most commonly arising in the vertebral column and the long bones, with a higher incidence in the first decades of life and a female predilection. Rarely, ABCs involve the head and neck region, making up 2% to 3% of cases, with the mandible being the most affected site. The exact etiopathogenesis remains unclear, with proposed theories including trauma, vascular anomalies, genetic predisposition, and circulatory disturbances. ABCs may occur as primary lesions or in association with other bone pathologies, such as ossifying fibroma, chondroblastoma, solitary bone cyst, giant cell tumor, and osteoblastoma.1 ABCs are classified into 3 types. The vascular type, which is most common, presents with rapid onset of painful swelling and expansile mass, often associated with pathological fracture and substantial intraoperative bleeding. Histologically, it shows blood-filled spaces separated by fibrous septa containing fibroblasts, osteoclastlike giant cells, and reactive woven bone.2The solid variant, as in this case, develops gradually, manifesting as firm swelling with mild pain. Microscopically, it demonstrates a predominance of fibroblastic proliferation with scattered giant cells and osteoid formation, while cystic blood spaces are few or absent. The mixed type combines features of both.3 ABCs can be difficult to diagnose because of overlapping radiographic and histological features with other primary bone pathologies. ABCs often present as expansile, lytic lesions with septations and cortical thinning, and may demonstrate fluid-fluid levels on magnetic resonance imaging, though not pathognomonic. Osteoblastoma commonly resembles ABCs initially but matures to mixed radiolucent-radiopaque appearance with calcification. In comparison, central giant cell granuloma (CGCG) typically appears as a fusiform radiolucency with variable cortical erosion, a pattern that is radiographically indistinguishable from osteitis fibrosa cystica, also known as brown tumors.4Notably in this case, odontogenic pathology was not considered in the differential because these lesions generally arise above the inferior alveolar canal and are tooth associated. A comprehensive diagnostic approach with laboratory testing and biopsy confirmation is essential. Laboratory studies aid in distinguishing brown tumors, characterized by elevated serum calcium and parathyroid hormone.5Conventional histology usually suffices to diagnose osteoblastoma, characterized by trabeculae of woven bone lined by active osteoblasts.6However, fluorescence in situ hybridization analysis may be required to distinguish ABCs from CGCGs when conventional study is inconclusive. About 70% of primary ABCs demonstrateUSP6rearrangements (Figure 2), while CGCG may harbor variations in genes such asLRP1BandNOTCH4.7,8 ABCs can be managed through various treatment approaches. The preference is toward surgical excision whenever possible due to its high rate of complete healing and relatively low risk of recurrence. In recent years, there has been growing interest in less invasive options. Percutaneous sclerotherapy with agents such as doxycycline or polidocanol has shown promising results. Other modalities, including embolization, bisphosphonate therapy, and radiotherapy, may also be considered in select cases.9 In conclusion, accurate diagnosis of ABCs is essential, as management strategies differ substantially. ABCs are aggressive lesions typically treated with curettage, surgical excision, sclerotherapy or embolization, whereas brown tumors improve with management of hyperparathyroidism. In contrast, CGCGs, depending on the subtype, may respond to intralesional corticosteroids or denosumab in addition to surgical excision.10The patient in this case is doing well after surgical resection and alloplast jawline reconstruction without issue and is currently 1 year out from surgery without evidence of disease recurrence.

case_info.explanation: An aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC) is a benign lesion most commonly arising in the vertebral column and the long bones, with a higher incidence in the first decades of life and a female predilection. Rarely, ABCs involve the head and neck region, making up 2% to 3% of cases, with the mandible being the most affected site. The exact etiopathogenesis remains unclear, with proposed theories including trauma, vascular anomalies, genetic predisposition, and circulatory disturbances. ABCs may occur as primary lesions or in association with other bone pathologies, such as ossifying fibroma, chondroblastoma, solitary bone cyst, giant cell tumor, and osteoblastoma.1 ABCs are classified into 3 types. The vascular type, which is most common, presents with rapid onset of painful swelling and expansile mass, often associated with pathological fracture and substantial intraoperative bleeding. Histologically, it shows blood-filled spaces separated by fibrous septa containing fibroblasts, osteoclastlike giant cells, and reactive woven bone.2The solid variant, as in this case, develops gradually, manifesting as firm swelling with mild pain. Microscopically, it demonstrates a predominance of fibroblastic proliferation with scattered giant cells and osteoid formation, while cystic blood spaces are few or absent. The mixed type combines features of both.3 ABCs can be difficult to diagnose because of overlapping radiographic and histological features with other primary bone pathologies. ABCs often present as expansile, lytic lesions with septations and cortical thinning, and may demonstrate fluid-fluid levels on magnetic resonance imaging, though not pathognomonic. Osteoblastoma commonly resembles ABCs initially but matures to mixed radiolucent-radiopaque appearance with calcification. In comparison, central giant cell granuloma (CGCG) typically appears as a fusiform radiolucency with variable cortical erosion, a pattern that is radiographically indistinguishable from osteitis fibrosa cystica, also known as brown tumors.4Notably in this case, odontogenic pathology was not considered in the differential because these lesions generally arise above the inferior alveolar canal and are tooth associated. A comprehensive diagnostic approach with laboratory testing and biopsy confirmation is essential. Laboratory studies aid in distinguishing brown tumors, characterized by elevated serum calcium and parathyroid hormone.5Conventional histology usually suffices to diagnose osteoblastoma, characterized by trabeculae of woven bone lined by active osteoblasts.6However, fluorescence in situ hybridization analysis may be required to distinguish ABCs from CGCGs when conventional study is inconclusive. About 70% of primary ABCs demonstrateUSP6rearrangements (Figure 2), while CGCG may harbor variations in genes such asLRP1BandNOTCH4.7,8 ABCs can be managed through various treatment approaches. The preference is toward surgical excision whenever possible due to its high rate of complete healing and relatively low risk of recurrence. In recent years, there has been growing interest in less invasive options. Percutaneous sclerotherapy with agents such as doxycycline or polidocanol has shown promising results. Other modalities, including embolization, bisphosphonate therapy, and radiotherapy, may also be considered in select cases.9 In conclusion, accurate diagnosis of ABCs is essential, as management strategies differ substantially. ABCs are aggressive lesions typically treated with curettage, surgical excision, sclerotherapy or embolization, whereas brown tumors improve with management of hyperparathyroidism. In contrast, CGCGs, depending on the subtype, may respond to intralesional corticosteroids or denosumab in addition to surgical excision.10The patient in this case is doing well after surgical resection and alloplast jawline reconstruction without issue and is currently 1 year out from surgery without evidence of disease recurrence.

case_info.explanation: An aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC) is a benign lesion most commonly arising in the vertebral column and the long bones, with a higher incidence in the first decades of life and a female predilection. Rarely, ABCs involve the head and neck region, making up 2% to 3% of cases, with the mandible being the most affected site. The exact etiopathogenesis remains unclear, with proposed theories including trauma, vascular anomalies, genetic predisposition, and circulatory disturbances. ABCs may occur as primary lesions or in association with other bone pathologies, such as ossifying fibroma, chondroblastoma, solitary bone cyst, giant cell tumor, and osteoblastoma.1 ABCs are classified into 3 types. The vascular type, which is most common, presents with rapid onset of painful swelling and expansile mass, often associated with pathological fracture and substantial intraoperative bleeding. Histologically, it shows blood-filled spaces separated by fibrous septa containing fibroblasts, osteoclastlike giant cells, and reactive woven bone.2The solid variant, as in this case, develops gradually, manifesting as firm swelling with mild pain. Microscopically, it demonstrates a predominance of fibroblastic proliferation with scattered giant cells and osteoid formation, while cystic blood spaces are few or absent. The mixed type combines features of both.3 ABCs can be difficult to diagnose because of overlapping radiographic and histological features with other primary bone pathologies. ABCs often present as expansile, lytic lesions with septations and cortical thinning, and may demonstrate fluid-fluid levels on magnetic resonance imaging, though not pathognomonic. Osteoblastoma commonly resembles ABCs initially but matures to mixed radiolucent-radiopaque appearance with calcification. In comparison, central giant cell granuloma (CGCG) typically appears as a fusiform radiolucency with variable cortical erosion, a pattern that is radiographically indistinguishable from osteitis fibrosa cystica, also known as brown tumors.4Notably in this case, odontogenic pathology was not considered in the differential because these lesions generally arise above the inferior alveolar canal and are tooth associated. A comprehensive diagnostic approach with laboratory testing and biopsy confirmation is essential. Laboratory studies aid in distinguishing brown tumors, characterized by elevated serum calcium and parathyroid hormone.5Conventional histology usually suffices to diagnose osteoblastoma, characterized by trabeculae of woven bone lined by active osteoblasts.6However, fluorescence in situ hybridization analysis may be required to distinguish ABCs from CGCGs when conventional study is inconclusive. About 70% of primary ABCs demonstrateUSP6rearrangements (Figure 2), while CGCG may harbor variations in genes such asLRP1BandNOTCH4.7,8 ABCs can be managed through various treatment approaches. The preference is toward surgical excision whenever possible due to its high rate of complete healing and relatively low risk of recurrence. In recent years, there has been growing interest in less invasive options. Percutaneous sclerotherapy with agents such as doxycycline or polidocanol has shown promising results. Other modalities, including embolization, bisphosphonate therapy, and radiotherapy, may also be considered in select cases.9 In conclusion, accurate diagnosis of ABCs is essential, as management strategies differ substantially. ABCs are aggressive lesions typically treated with curettage, surgical excision, sclerotherapy or embolization, whereas brown tumors improve with management of hyperparathyroidism. In contrast, CGCGs, depending on the subtype, may respond to intralesional corticosteroids or denosumab in addition to surgical excision.10The patient in this case is doing well after surgical resection and alloplast jawline reconstruction without issue and is currently 1 year out from surgery without evidence of disease recurrence.

case_info.explanation: An aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC) is a benign lesion most commonly arising in the vertebral column and the long bones, with a higher incidence in the first decades of life and a female predilection. Rarely, ABCs involve the head and neck region, making up 2% to 3% of cases, with the mandible being the most affected site. The exact etiopathogenesis remains unclear, with proposed theories including trauma, vascular anomalies, genetic predisposition, and circulatory disturbances. ABCs may occur as primary lesions or in association with other bone pathologies, such as ossifying fibroma, chondroblastoma, solitary bone cyst, giant cell tumor, and osteoblastoma.1 ABCs are classified into 3 types. The vascular type, which is most common, presents with rapid onset of painful swelling and expansile mass, often associated with pathological fracture and substantial intraoperative bleeding. Histologically, it shows blood-filled spaces separated by fibrous septa containing fibroblasts, osteoclastlike giant cells, and reactive woven bone.2The solid variant, as in this case, develops gradually, manifesting as firm swelling with mild pain. Microscopically, it demonstrates a predominance of fibroblastic proliferation with scattered giant cells and osteoid formation, while cystic blood spaces are few or absent. The mixed type combines features of both.3 ABCs can be difficult to diagnose because of overlapping radiographic and histological features with other primary bone pathologies. ABCs often present as expansile, lytic lesions with septations and cortical thinning, and may demonstrate fluid-fluid levels on magnetic resonance imaging, though not pathognomonic. Osteoblastoma commonly resembles ABCs initially but matures to mixed radiolucent-radiopaque appearance with calcification. In comparison, central giant cell granuloma (CGCG) typically appears as a fusiform radiolucency with variable cortical erosion, a pattern that is radiographically indistinguishable from osteitis fibrosa cystica, also known as brown tumors.4Notably in this case, odontogenic pathology was not considered in the differential because these lesions generally arise above the inferior alveolar canal and are tooth associated. A comprehensive diagnostic approach with laboratory testing and biopsy confirmation is essential. Laboratory studies aid in distinguishing brown tumors, characterized by elevated serum calcium and parathyroid hormone.5Conventional histology usually suffices to diagnose osteoblastoma, characterized by trabeculae of woven bone lined by active osteoblasts.6However, fluorescence in situ hybridization analysis may be required to distinguish ABCs from CGCGs when conventional study is inconclusive. About 70% of primary ABCs demonstrateUSP6rearrangements (Figure 2), while CGCG may harbor variations in genes such asLRP1BandNOTCH4.7,8 ABCs can be managed through various treatment approaches. The preference is toward surgical excision whenever possible due to its high rate of complete healing and relatively low risk of recurrence. In recent years, there has been growing interest in less invasive options. Percutaneous sclerotherapy with agents such as doxycycline or polidocanol has shown promising results. Other modalities, including embolization, bisphosphonate therapy, and radiotherapy, may also be considered in select cases.9 In conclusion, accurate diagnosis of ABCs is essential, as management strategies differ substantially. ABCs are aggressive lesions typically treated with curettage, surgical excision, sclerotherapy or embolization, whereas brown tumors improve with management of hyperparathyroidism. In contrast, CGCGs, depending on the subtype, may respond to intralesional corticosteroids or denosumab in addition to surgical excision.10The patient in this case is doing well after surgical resection and alloplast jawline reconstruction without issue and is currently 1 year out from surgery without evidence of disease recurrence.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition:

   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid

case_info.explanation: An aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC) is a benign lesion most commonly arising in the vertebral column and the long bones, with a higher incidence in the first decades of life and a female predilection. Rarely, ABCs involve the head and neck region, making up 2% to 3% of cases, with the mandible being the most affected site. The exact etiopathogenesis remains unclear, with proposed theories including trauma, vascular anomalies, genetic predisposition, and circulatory disturbances. ABCs may occur as primary lesions or in association with other bone pathologies, such as ossifying fibroma, chondroblastoma, solitary bone cyst, giant cell tumor, and osteoblastoma.1 ABCs are classified into 3 types. The vascular type, which is most common, presents with rapid onset of painful swelling and expansile mass, often associated with pathological fracture and substantial intraoperative bleeding. Histologically, it shows blood-filled spaces separated by fibrous septa containing fibroblasts, osteoclastlike giant cells, and reactive woven bone.2The solid variant, as in this case, develops gradually, manifesting as firm swelling with mild pain. Microscopically, it demonstrates a predominance of fibroblastic proliferation with scattered giant cells and osteoid formation, while cystic blood spaces are few or absent. The mixed type combines features of both.3 ABCs can be difficult to diagnose because of overlapping radiographic and histological features with other primary bone pathologies. ABCs often present as expansile, lytic lesions with septations and cortical thinning, and may demonstrate fluid-fluid levels on magnetic resonance imaging, though not pathognomonic. Osteoblastoma commonly resembles ABCs initially but matures to mixed radiolucent-radiopaque appearance with calcification. In comparison, central giant cell granuloma (CGCG) typically appears as a fusiform radiolucency with variable cortical erosion, a pattern that is radiographically indistinguishable from osteitis fibrosa cystica, also known as brown tumors.4Notably in this case, odontogenic pathology was not considered in the differential because these lesions generally arise above the inferior alveolar canal and are tooth associated. A comprehensive diagnostic approach with laboratory testing and biopsy confirmation is essential. Laboratory studies aid in distinguishing brown tumors, characterized by elevated serum calcium and parathyroid hormone.5Conventional histology usually suffices to diagnose osteoblastoma, characterized by trabeculae of woven bone lined by active osteoblasts.6However, fluorescence in situ hybridization analysis may be required to distinguish ABCs from CGCGs when conventional study is inconclusive. About 70% of primary ABCs demonstrateUSP6rearrangements (Figure 2), while CGCG may harbor variations in genes such asLRP1BandNOTCH4.7,8 ABCs can be managed through various treatment approaches. The preference is toward surgical excision whenever possible due to its high rate of complete healing and relatively low risk of recurrence. In recent years, there has been growing interest in less invasive options. Percutaneous sclerotherapy with agents such as doxycycline or polidocanol has shown promising results. Other modalities, including embolization, bisphosphonate therapy, and radiotherapy, may also be considered in select cases.9 In conclusion, accurate diagnosis of ABCs is essential, as management strategies differ substantially. ABCs are aggressive lesions typically treated with curettage, surgical excision, sclerotherapy or embolization, whereas brown tumors improve with management of hyperparathyroidism. In contrast, CGCGs, depending on the subtype, may respond to intralesional corticosteroids or denosumab in addition to surgical excision.10The patient in this case is doing well after surgical resection and alloplast jawline reconstruction without issue and is currently 1 year out from surgery without evidence of disease recurrence.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: An aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC) is a benign lesion most commonly arising in the vertebral column and the long bones, with a higher incidence in the first decades of life and a female predilection. Rarely, ABCs involve the head and neck region, making up 2% to 3% of cases, with the mandible being the most affected site. The exact etiopathogenesis remains unclear, with proposed theories including trauma, vascular anomalies, genetic predisposition, and circulatory disturbances. ABCs may occur as primary lesions or in association with other bone pathologies, such as ossifying fibroma, chondroblastoma, solitary bone cyst, giant cell tumor, and osteoblastoma.1 ABCs are classified into 3 types. The vascular type, which is most common, presents with rapid onset of painful swelling and expansile mass, often associated with pathological fracture and substantial intraoperative bleeding. Histologically, it shows blood-filled spaces separated by fibrous septa containing fibroblasts, osteoclastlike giant cells, and reactive woven bone.2The solid variant, as in this case, develops gradually, manifesting as firm swelling with mild pain. Microscopically, it demonstrates a predominance of fibroblastic proliferation with scattered giant cells and osteoid formation, while cystic blood spaces are few or absent. The mixed type combines features of both.3 ABCs can be difficult to diagnose because of overlapping radiographic and histological features with other primary bone pathologies. ABCs often present as expansile, lytic lesions with septations and cortical thinning, and may demonstrate fluid-fluid levels on magnetic resonance imaging, though not pathognomonic. Osteoblastoma commonly resembles ABCs initially but matures to mixed radiolucent-radiopaque appearance with calcification. In comparison, central giant cell granuloma (CGCG) typically appears as a fusiform radiolucency with variable cortical erosion, a pattern that is radiographically indistinguishable from osteitis fibrosa cystica, also known as brown tumors.4Notably in this case, odontogenic pathology was not considered in the differential because these lesions generally arise above the inferior alveolar canal and are tooth associated. A comprehensive diagnostic approach with laboratory testing and biopsy confirmation is essential. Laboratory studies aid in distinguishing brown tumors, characterized by elevated serum calcium and parathyroid hormone.5Conventional histology usually suffices to diagnose osteoblastoma, characterized by trabeculae of woven bone lined by active osteoblasts.6However, fluorescence in situ hybridization analysis may be required to distinguish ABCs from CGCGs when conventional study is inconclusive. About 70% of primary ABCs demonstrateUSP6rearrangements (Figure 2), while CGCG may harbor variations in genes such asLRP1BandNOTCH4.7,8 ABCs can be managed through various treatment approaches. The preference is toward surgical excision whenever possible due to its high rate of complete healing and relatively low risk of recurrence. In recent years, there has been growing interest in less invasive options. Percutaneous sclerotherapy with agents such as doxycycline or polidocanol has shown promising results. Other modalities, including embolization, bisphosphonate therapy, and radiotherapy, may also be considered in select cases.9 In conclusion, accurate diagnosis of ABCs is essential, as management strategies differ substantially. ABCs are aggressive lesions typically treated with curettage, surgical excision, sclerotherapy or embolization, whereas brown tumors improve with management of hyperparathyroidism. In contrast, CGCGs, depending on the subtype, may respond to intralesional corticosteroids or denosumab in addition to surgical excision.10The patient in this case is doing well after surgical resection and alloplast jawline reconstruction without issue and is currently 1 year out from surgery without evidence of disease recurrence.

case_info.explanation: An aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC) is a benign lesion most commonly arising in the vertebral column and the long bones, with a higher incidence in the first decades of life and a female predilection. Rarely, ABCs involve the head and neck region, making up 2% to 3% of cases, with the mandible being the most affected site. The exact etiopathogenesis remains unclear, with proposed theories including trauma, vascular anomalies, genetic predisposition, and circulatory disturbances. ABCs may occur as primary lesions or in association with other bone pathologies, such as ossifying fibroma, chondroblastoma, solitary bone cyst, giant cell tumor, and osteoblastoma.1 ABCs are classified into 3 types. The vascular type, which is most common, presents with rapid onset of painful swelling and expansile mass, often associated with pathological fracture and substantial intraoperative bleeding. Histologically, it shows blood-filled spaces separated by fibrous septa containing fibroblasts, osteoclastlike giant cells, and reactive woven bone.2The solid variant, as in this case, develops gradually, manifesting as firm swelling with mild pain. Microscopically, it demonstrates a predominance of fibroblastic proliferation with scattered giant cells and osteoid formation, while cystic blood spaces are few or absent. The mixed type combines features of both.3 ABCs can be difficult to diagnose because of overlapping radiographic and histological features with other primary bone pathologies. ABCs often present as expansile, lytic lesions with septations and cortical thinning, and may demonstrate fluid-fluid levels on magnetic resonance imaging, though not pathognomonic. Osteoblastoma commonly resembles ABCs initially but matures to mixed radiolucent-radiopaque appearance with calcification. In comparison, central giant cell granuloma (CGCG) typically appears as a fusiform radiolucency with variable cortical erosion, a pattern that is radiographically indistinguishable from osteitis fibrosa cystica, also known as brown tumors.4Notably in this case, odontogenic pathology was not considered in the differential because these lesions generally arise above the inferior alveolar canal and are tooth associated. A comprehensive diagnostic approach with laboratory testing and biopsy confirmation is essential. case_info.explanation: An aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC) is a benign lesion most commonly arising in the vertebral column and the long bones, with a higher incidence in the first decades of life and a female predilection. Rarely, ABCs involve the head and neck region, making up 2% to 3% of cases, with the mandible being the most affected site. The exact etiopathogenesis remains unclear, with proposed theories including trauma, vascular anomalies, genetic predisposition, and circulatory disturbances. ABCs may occur as primary lesions or in association with other bone pathologies, such as ossifying fibroma, chondroblastoma, solitary bone cyst, giant cell tumor, and osteoblastoma.1 ABCs are classified into 3 types. The vascular type, which is most common, presents with rapid onset of painful swelling and expansile mass, often associated with pathological fracture and substantial intraoperative bleeding. Histologically, it shows blood-filled spaces separated by fibrous septa containing fibroblasts, osteoclastlike giant cells, and reactive woven bone.2The solid variant, as in this case, develops gradually, manifesting as firm swelling with mild pain. Microscopically, it demonstrates a predominance of fibroblastic proliferation with scattered giant cells and osteoid formation, while cystic blood spaces are few or absent. The mixed type combines features of both.3 ABCs can be difficult to diagnose because of overlapping radiographic and histological features with other primary bone pathologies. ABCs often present as expansile, lytic lesions with septations and cortical thinning, and may demonstrate fluid-fluid levels on magnetic resonance imaging, though not pathognomonic. Osteoblastoma commonly resembles ABCs initially but matures to mixed radiolucent-radiopaque appearance with calcification. In comparison, central giant cell granuloma (CGCG) typically appears as a fusiform radiolucency with variable cortical erosion, a pattern that is radiographically indistinguishable from osteitis fibrosa cystica, also known as brown tumors.4Notably in this case, odontogenic pathology was not considered in the differential because these lesions generally arise above the inferior alveolar canal and are tooth associated. A comprehensive diagnostic approach with laboratory testing and biopsy confirmation is essential. Laboratory studies aid in distinguishing brown tumors, characterized by elevated serum calcium and parathyroid hormone.5Conventional histology usually suffices to diagnose osteoblastoma, characterized by trabeculae of woven bone lined by active osteoblasts.6However, fluorescence in situ hybridization analysis may be required to distinguish ABCs from CGCGs when conventional study is inconclusive. About 70% of primary ABCs demonstrateUSP6rearrangements (Figure 2), while CGCG may harbor variations in genes such asLRP1BandNOTCH4.7,8 ABCs can be managed through various treatment approaches. The preference is toward surgical excision whenever possible due to its high rate of complete healing and relatively low risk of recurrence. In recent years, there has been growing interest in less invasive options. Percutaneous sclerotherapy with agents such as doxycycline or polidocanol has shown promising results. Other modalities, including embolization, bisphosphonate therapy, and radiotherapy, may also be considered in select cases.9 In conclusion, accurate diagnosis of ABCs is essential, as management strategies differ substantially. ABCs are aggressive lesions typically treated with curettage, surgical excision, sclerotherapy or embolization, whereas brown tumors improve with management of hyperparathyroidism. In contrast, CGCGs, depending on the subtype, may respond to intralesional corticosteroids or denosumab in addition to surgical excision.10The patient in this case is doing well after surgical resection and alloplast jawline reconstruction without issue and is currently 1 year out from surgery without evidence of disease recurrence.

the best decision, at the lowest cognitive cost to the clinician. You control HOW the AI speaks,
never WHAT the medical answer is (that is the AI's job). Each turn you choose ONE control stage and
write a short guidance instruction for the AI's next utterance.

The 3 control stages (pick exactly one, and only from the reachable list you are given):

- EXPAND  — cheap, safe, broadens the picture. Elicit the clinician's reasoning, ask them to
            justify, or surface a missing goal/criterion/perspective. Do NOT yet evaluate or push
            an option. Effect is often delayed (sets up a later CHALLENGE). Use when the state is
            unclear or the clinician hasn't exposed their rationale.
- CHALLENGE — expensive and highest-yield, but also most likely to make the clinician regress.
            Directly evaluate the option on the table against a goal/criterion, or contrast two
            options, and press the clinician to engage the mismatch. Spend it deliberately: when
            you have reason to think the clinician's current position is wrong or under-examined.
- CONVERGE — cheap, terminal. Recommend the now-best-supported option and invite accept/reject,
            or confirm an agreement already reached. This is the STOP / pacing lever — stop
            spending burden once belief has settled.

Output STRICT JSON only:
{{
  "stage": "EXPAND | CHALLENGE | CONVERGE",
  "reason": "one short sentence: the hidden state you infer and why this stage now",
  "action_guidance": "concrete HOW-instruction for the AI's next utterance (no option letter/answer)"
}}

She had multiple prior emergency department encounters for this lesion, and maxillofacial computed tomography revealed a multiloculated radiolucent lesion situated below the inferior alveolar nerve at the right mandibular angle (Figure 1B). On clinical examination, there was firm, tender external swelling of the right gonial angle along the inferior border. Intraoral findings were unremarkable, with no drainage or evident expansion into the retromolar trigone. An incisional biopsy was performed via a transoral approach. The intralesional content appeared to be dark brown and spongy.
